paragraphs: Some of what he has said reproduces argumentation we have already treated and refuted. We turn now to the additional material — that which has not yet been answered. As to his statement that the Wise One does not leave His command and prohibition ambiguous (deploying Deut 30:11, "it is not hidden from thee," and Prov 8:9, "they are all right for the understanding") — this is our own statement, and is one of the things by which qiyās itself is established. For his claim — that the law is clear and unhidden — only means that if you investigate with sound investigation, free from partiality, and use qiyās in its proper mode, the realities of the farāʾiḍ will be uncovered for you, and nothing among them will be hidden.

As to the seven foundational reasons he claimed compel us to naql — and his examples of the fringes and the sukkah: What his school says about the sukkah is contrary to what Scripture itself describes in the narrative of Ezra (Neh 8:13–18). And as to the fringes: while his school presented themselves as if they had the kayfiyya settled by transmission, they have in fact blocked themselves on this and contradicted themselves. They claim that the tekhelet (blue) was a specific gemstone-derived substance, and they then admit that they no longer know what that substance is.[{2}] So on their own logic, the fringe-obligation has now fallen off the community for this age, since the means of its completion is missing. By parallel: they also hold that purity from the dead has fallen off this age, since the purification-water by which the rite is to be completed is missing.

As to his point on the quantity of the terumah: if we do not know it in this age, we have no need to know it — for the very recipient (the priest) is currently not identified; and if we ever did need to know it, investigation would extract it by qiyās, just as it has extracted many other things not explicit in the text. So too on what he mentioned of what the king is forbidden to multiply — wives, horses, money. Scripture itself has attached to each of these three things a qualifier that gives the sense:[{3}] — On horses (Deut 17:16): "lest he cause the people to return to Egypt." So what is forbidden is the multiplication that would require a return to Egypt; if he owns horses not by way of returning to Egypt, that is not forbidden. Solomon's narrative confirms this. — On wives (Deut 17:17): "lest his heart go astray." So what is forbidden is multiplication that would cause his heart to go astray. Whether two, three, or a thousand — if his heart strays, it is forbidden; if not, not. — On money (Deut 17:17): "[silver and gold] he shall not multiply to himself excessively." Possibly this is a parallel to v. 20, "lest his heart be lifted up above his brethren" — so what is forbidden is self-aggrandizement over his fellow Israelites; or possibly it is a prohibition against committing one's efforts to amassing money so as to neglect the obligations of knowing the law. The phrase "excessively" (meʾod) in v. 17 supports the latter. Solomon, who acquired immense wealth without seeking it, was not censured for this; what is forbidden is the toil of seeking — not the wealth itself.

As to his statement about the knowledge of the Sabbath — by my life, that indeed is known only by report and naql; and it has parallels, which we will treat below. So too his statement about the prohibited works on the Sabbath. But al-Fayyūmī should be embarrassed to mention this bab. For his own school have licensed on the Sabbath things that sense itself (let alone reason) attests to be corruption — and in contradiction with themselves. They have, for instance, licensed cooking and roasting on the Sabbath, and the leaving of fire burning, while forbidding the kindling of fires; they license the preparation of mills before the Sabbath and the leaving them running into the Sabbath; we have already mentioned (and will mention more) of these in detail. So too their licensing of sewing-with-a-thread and writing of letters; their teaching that "one may not move one's spittle in one's mouth for four cubits" (which we already mentioned); their teaching that "the Sabbath is suspended for [the circumcision of] an infant but not for David the king of Israel"; and their teaching at m. Shabbat 23:1 — "a man may borrow from his fellow"[{4}] — and so on, beyond number.

As to his point on the vessel that admits impurity — we have already mentioned what occurred between Eliezer b. Hyrcanus and the rest of the Rabbanites in their disagreement on this matter; and the proof on Eliezer's side via the appearance of miracles, with God Himself (mighty and exalted) testifying for him. This case alone refutes everything al-Fayyūmī and others claim about ijmāʿ and Rabbanite naql; indeed, it is a scandal against the whole of them, on any hearing.[{5}] As for our own co-religionists from the Ananites and the Qaraʾites — they have spoken on this matter with strong and decisive language and made clear which vessel is to be regarded as susceptible to impurity. We will mention this in its proper place.

As to prayer: the obligation of it is plain in Scripture, in several places in the Torah and the Prophets. The Rabbanites have mentioned some of these, and have relied on Daniel's narrative (Dan 6:11) to ground the count of three daily prayers; we will explain this in our discussion of prayer. We have also noted previously that the Rabbanites have abolished certain obligatory prayers and have imposed prayers that are not obligatory.

As to chronology from the Second Temple onward: this is not a matter of religious benefit — were we ignorant of it, no harm would come — and besides, knowledge of it can be had from other than the Rabbanites.

As to his case from the Messiah and the bishārāt: that without Rabbanite interpretation, one might think that all the eschatological promises had already been fulfilled in the days of some earlier king — this is mere assertion. The matter is too plain to admit such doubt. If someone objects: "but on your view, the Christians and others among the Jewish sects have made this kind of claim" — we reply: the Christians' making this claim is no more probative than their claim that God is one jawhar of three aqānīm, or their claim that the Torah has been abrogated. The same applies to others — like Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (who claimed prophecy) and Yudghan (who claimed messiahship); we will demonstrate the falsity of all their claims later, not on the basis of naql but on the basis of clear scriptural evidences. It can also be said to him who deploys this objection: we do not find that naql prevented these groups from making their claims. So if his case were as he supposes, the naql would have stopped the Christians and the Iṣfahānīs from making the claims they made. Moreover, the bishārāt that Scripture mentions as occurring in the days of the Messiah — Scripture did not attach them to fixed years or known dates. So our knowing the historical date would be irrelevant to what he claims.

As to his account of how the naql came to be transmitted, his story that the Torah was written in the fortieth year, and so forth, and his claim that the kings and priests preserved the oral tradition while in the Holy Land — this is our position too, and we will explain it further later. As to his account of how the sages turned to the heads of the hidden science and inscribed them as Mishnah, then the disciples inscribed the remaining branches as Talmud — we have already laid out the refutation of this in Bab 13, and need not repeat ourselves.

As to his attempt to exempt himself from what is binding upon him in the matter of dicta in the Mishnah and Talmud ascribed to specific individuals — and his claim that those individuals were the ones who reminded the community of the rules, not their originators — his comparison of this to Scripture's ascription of Num 31:23 to Eleazar: His statement here itself indicates that these statements ascribed to specific individuals were forgotten by the community as a whole, until each of these individuals reminded the community of one or another of them. If, however, the community as a whole had forgotten these statements such that they had to be re-reminded — we cannot be sure that they have not also forgotten things that no one happened to remind them of, things that have simply fallen away and been lost. And that is itself evidence that the naql has lapsed and been broken.

He then sensed what was binding on him from the disagreement of the people of the Mishnah and Talmud, so he claimed that the disagreement is not real but reduces to the three kinds we have summarized. The minimum reply: even if it were as he says, even if the original disagreement were not real — the result was that the community settled on disagreement in fact. The disciples of Beit Hillel and the disciples of Beit Shammai did end up at the point of one school killing some of the other; the schools of Shām and ʿIrāq did establish themselves in opposition on the matters we have detailed, with each school explicitly holding that the other has departed from the religion. This is again the bone in the throat of al-Fayyūmī and of every other claimant of Rabbanite naql. We will mention later some of their attempted resolutions of this disagreement, and demonstrate their corruption.

A more remarkable case still: the ancient Rabbanites — all of them — held that one who touches a corpse becomes impure for seven days; that one who touches that person is also impure for seven days; that one who touches the third in the chain is impure for one day only. They grounded this on Num 19:22: "And every thing that the unclean person touches shall be unclean … and the person (nefesh) that touches him shall be unclean until the evening." They read the verse: the unclean person = the one who touched the corpse; unclean = impure for seven days; the person who touches him = the third-degree contact, impure for one day only. Then Yose b. Yoezer, a man of Tzeredah, came along and changed this on them, saying what we now say: namely, that one who touches a corpse is impure for seven days, and one who touches that person is impure for one day only (with the third-degree contact not impure at all).[{6}] Are they not ashamed, with this on their record, to invoke naql?

As to his statement that he will mention the four materials of qiyās: we have already presented and refuted these (Bab 10). As to his point that some of his school make the non-acceptance of part of the community a critique of the naql-claim — and his rebuttal that on this logic, refusal to accept the written would equally be a critique — the two cases are not symmetric. Those who reject this so-called naql reject it on the strength of proofs and evidences of its corruption, plus the self-contradictions we have noted, and they are a vast community. By contrast, those who have rejected the written Torah are a few isolated individuals who appear here and there sporadically with no following; some of them take their position from groups already outside Judaism — e.g., Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī, who took his contrary positions on the written Torah from the Samaritans (who are outside the religion altogether). His followers in his day were a tiny group; they then died out and their position collapsed. As to his claim that some of his school make the failure to memorize the transmitted material a critique of the tradition — and his rebuttal that the same would apply to memorization of the written — this is not what our companions in fact say. What they say is precisely what we have already laid out: naql must be in the hands of the entire community, or at least the majority — like the Sabbath-day knowledge and similar things that are in everyone's hands. The "naql" claimed by Rabbanites is only in the hands of a small group, ascribed only to them: even when one of them dissents, his fellows say of him "this man dissents from the Rabbanites" — not "this man dissents from God or His Torah"; not even "this man dissents from the transmitters." The very term al-nāqila (the transmitters) as a designation for this school is a recent invention. By my life, it is a clever stratagem — if it had been substantively founded. We have already, before reporting al-Fayyūmī, mentioned in passing a question that establishes qiyās and overthrows the naql-claim, and from which there is no escape — by which all that al-Fayyūmī and others have said about naql is refuted. We will now (in Bab 16 and following) take up the position of Yaʿqūb b. Efraim al-Shāmī, who claimed that both the Palestinian and Babylonian disagreement-positions are correct, and that God ordained the worship by two opposing schools at once. ---
